title: PostgreSQL: replication & availability
description: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication, read replicas, replication lag and read-your-writes, and how failover works.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: What does asynchronous replication, the default, do on commit?

options.text: Confirms to the client immediately and sends changes to replicas afterwards.
options.why: Right: fast but replicas lag.

options.text: Waits for at least one replica to acknowledge before confirming.
options.why: That describes synchronous replication.

options.text: Rejects writes until all replicas are fully caught up.
options.why: Neither mode behaves like this.

options.text: Stops replicating whenever the primary is busy.
options.why: Replication continues in the background.

questions.explanation: Async maximises write speed but allows a window of lost writes if the primary dies before replicas catch up.

questions.prompt: What is the trade-off of synchronous replication?

options.text: Stronger durability across nodes, paid for with higher write latency.
options.why: Right: every commit waits on a replica.

options.text: Lower write latency and weaker durability.
options.why: It is the opposite.

options.text: No cost, because replicas are free to wait for most everyday workloads.
options.why: The primary's clients feel the wait.

options.text: It only works if the replica is in a different region in a typical production setup.
options.why: Location is not a requirement, though distance raises the cost.

questions.explanation: A hybrid is common: one or two synchronous replicas for safety, more asynchronous ones for read scaling.

questions.prompt: What do read replicas primarily buy you?

options.text: Read throughput that multiplies by the number of replicas.
options.why: Right: spread read queries across copies.

options.text: Write throughput that multiplies by the number of replicas.
options.why: All writes still go to the primary.

options.text: Elimination of every consistency concern.
options.why: Replication lag introduces new ones.

options.text: Automatic sharding of large tables.
options.why: Replicas are full copies, not shards.

questions.explanation: Send writes to the primary and reads to replicas: great for read-heavy products.

questions.prompt: A user posts, refreshes immediately and does not see the post. Which fix is most appropriate?

options.text: Route that user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write.
options.why: Right: restores read-your-writes without reading everything from the primary.

options.text: Remove all replicas and read only from the primary as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It removes the lag but throws away read scaling.

options.text: Tell the user to refresh until the post shows up.
options.why: That is a poor experience, not a design.

options.text: Switch the database to eventual consistency everywhere under normal operating conditions.
options.why: The lag is already eventual consistency; that is the problem.

questions.explanation: Replication lag is the key caveat. Pin recent writers to the primary or read from a replica that has caught up.

questions.prompt: True or false: a common setup keeps one or two synchronous replicas for durability and adds asynchronous replicas to scale reads.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: this hybrid is widely used.

options.text: False
options.why: It is a standard pattern, not an unsupported one.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL lets you choose which replicas are synchronous, so you can balance durability against write latency.

questions.prompt: When the primary fails, what is the rough failover sequence?

options.text: Detect the failure, promote a replica, update connection info, repoint applications.
options.why: Right: the standard four steps.

options.text: Delete the failed node and recreate every table from scratch in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Replicas already hold the data.

options.text: Pause all writes until an engineer restores a backup without any extra configuration.
options.why: Automatic failover avoids that.

options.text: Merge all replicas into one big table.
options.why: Replicas are copies; one is simply promoted.

questions.explanation: Managed services such as RDS or Cloud SQL automate this. Mention replication as reliability, not only scaling.
